blocks.text: It wasn't Andrés. It wasn't the clone. It was the woman from the hangar, the one who had said she would accept the no of a quayside, and who now had, instead of a quayside, a circle of metal.

blocks.text: Among her people she was called Nuria, an Earth name the seedbed had left them among others, which she had chosen without knowing that in Lo Pagán there had also been Nurias, in other centuries, beside this same water. She asked to cross. She asked standing up, without kneeling, faithful to the lesson of not turning the founder into an altar.

blocks.text: “I want to drink the plate,” she said. “If they send me back afterwards, I'll come back. If the water doesn't taste of what they put in my chip, I'll say so too. I'm not coming as an owner. I'm coming as someone checking a memory.”

blocks.text: Andrés, Aya and Lía waited in the warehouse at El Estacio, not in the kitchen: the house was not yet a car park for miracles. Helena had prevented the van at the door; she hadn't entirely prevented the machine, which was already there, discreet and enormous, breathing its dense silence. Lía stood beside the circle, her wrist awake, not to amend anything but to look, if she was asked.

blocks.text: The technician gave a signal. In the hangar, far away, Nuria stepped into the arch. Andrés, through the bridge, felt an instant of dissolving, not his own, borrowed: a cold, a brief disorder, the certainty that the body was ceasing to be a place. Then nothing. The bridge, with her, was cut. The original did not remain.

blocks.text: The time of the assembling was a while that felt to Aya like a levante: the coffee, had she had it to hand, would have been made again twice. Then, in the circle here, there was a weight. There was a woman. She had the fine scar beneath her nape, her eyes open, her mouth tense. She didn't scream. The first thing she asked for was air, and the air of this shore, which is neither quite sea nor quite land, entered her chest like a piece of news.

blocks.text: Lía didn't touch her yet.
blocks.html: Lía didn't touch her yet.

blocks.text: “What's your name?”
blocks.html: “What's your name?”

blocks.text: “Nuria,” she said, and the voice was a voice, not an appliance's echo. “I've crossed. Is this the water?”
blocks.html: “Nuria,” she said, and the voice was a voice, not an appliance's echo. “I've crossed. Is this the water?”

blocks.text: They took her to the promenade, slowly, the way you take someone who has just been born and is already an adult. The Mar Menor, at that hour, was a little dirty in one corner, beautiful everywhere else, with a crooked buoy. Nuria crouched, wet her fingers, raised them to her mouth. She cried, without theatre. Then she laughed, a laugh of confirmation.

blocks.text: “It tastes of salt, and of something the chip didn't quite know,” she said. “The chip was cleaner. This is better. This is alive.”
blocks.html: “It tastes of salt, and of something the chip didn't quite know,” she said. “The chip was cleaner. This is better. This is alive.”

blocks.text: Andrés, beside her, felt relief and a clean envy: she had set foot on what he had only drunk in letters, and she had done so being, or believing herself to be, the same woman who had been taken apart in a hangar.

blocks.text: “Does it hurt?” asked Lía.
blocks.html: “Does it hurt?” asked Lía.

blocks.text: “The hollow hurts,” said Nuria. “An instant when you don't belong anywhere. Afterwards you belong here. I remember the hangar, the half-built ship, the phrase, my name. I can't swear to you that the hollow hasn't taken something from me that I didn't know how to name. I can swear to you that I want a glass of this water, and that I'll ask your permission to drink it.”

blocks.text: They gave it to her in the cup that had crossed, which at last had a purpose. Aya, who had neither crossed nor received letters, watched her with a threshold attentiveness: another woman come from a workshop, not identical to her, and yet a sister of an origin.

blocks.text: “Welcome,” said Aya, and the word came out the way it had come out of Helena, years before, on the Moon, against part of her will. “This house isn't a company quayside. If you stay a while, I'll make you coffee. If you want to leave, the machine, they say, works in reverse too, when there's another one on the other side.”

blocks.text: Nuria nodded. She didn't stay to live. She stayed three days, slept in the room by the plot, walked El Estacio and El Carmolí, saw the gardens without owners, saw Vicente's door and didn't open it, because Lía told her who he had been, and a shut door, on this shore, was a fidelity. On the fourth day she asked to go back, to tell her people, and so that the hangar wouldn't be left with an absence and no story.

blocks.text: Before she stepped into the circle, Lía took her hand, with permission, and looked inside, not to amend. She saw a humanoid text, a chip, a memory of tablelands and, now, a new, salty layer from this plate. Her father's harbour wasn't there in her: she didn't receive letters; she had come in body.

blocks.text: “You're still you, as far as I can see,” said Lía. “What I can't see, you tell me, if one day you find it missing.”

blocks.text: “I'll tell you,” promised Nuria, and she was taken apart, and the warehouse once again had an empty chair, and the hangar, after a while, a weight called Nuria whose first request was to tell them about the taste.

blocks.text: When the clone's letter confirmed her arrival, Andrés sat down on the doorstep and Aya made him his coffee, cooled for half a minute.

blocks.text: “One has crossed and come back,” he said. “The water tasted of more than the chip to her. She talked about the hollow. If I cross, I'll have that hollow, and you'll have that empty chair. I still don't know whether I dare.”

blocks.text: Aya squeezed his fingers.
blocks.html: Aya squeezed his fingers.

blocks.text: “You don't dare today. Today we've welcomed a woman and said goodbye to her. That's enough for one week.”
blocks.html: “You don't dare today. Today we've welcomed a woman and said goodbye to her. That's enough for one week.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked:

blocks.text: *If a woman is taken apart and put together and asks for water, who did the asking: the one from there, the one from here, or the one from the hollow, who belongs nowhere? And if the water tastes of more than the memory, isn't that proof of a journey, or proof that the memory was less than the world?*

blocks.text: MAY, without judgment:
blocks.html: MAY, without judgment:

blocks.text: *A woman called Nuria has crossed from the hangar to El Estacio and gone back. She has drunk the Mar Menor. She has spoken of a hollow. She slept three nights at the plot. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: Lía, at the plot, washed the cup that had crossed and left it on the windowsill, empty, in the sun. It wasn't an altar. It was a tool that had already served a mouth. And tools, on this shore, are washed and offered again, if someone, once again, asks.
